features of EEG for emotion detection
Monira Islam1* and Tan Lee2 
Abstract 
Emotion is an integral part of human cognitive processes and behaviors. Automatic detection and classification 
of human emotion has been a goal of applied research. This study presents an approach to detecting emotion 
from multivariate electroencephalogram (EEG) with signal processing methods applied in the temporal, spec-
tral, and spatial domains. In this work, the noise-assisted multivariate empirical mode decomposition (NA-MEMD) 
is applied to EEG to extract a set of narrow-band intrinsic mode functions (IMF), upon which spectral analysis and spa-
tial connectivity analysis are performed. Applying Hilbert spectral analysis to those IMFs results in the marginal Hilbert 
spectrum (MHS). MHS is computed for each EEG channel to obtain the spectral energy of each segment. The spec-
tral energy across multiple EEG channels within the same segment is aggregated while the consecutive frames are 
stacked to give spectral-temporal feature representation. Again, connectivity analysis is performed at each instant 
with a non-linear measure named phase locking value (PLV) to construct the connectivity map containing spatial-
temporal features. A 2D CNN-BiLSTM is adopted to perform emotion detection with the MHS and the PLV features. 
On classifying high versus low states in valence, arousal, dominance, and liking, PLV showed better performance 
than MHS with 97.61%, 96.09%, 96.75%, and 97.23% accuracy, respectively, for DEAP dataset. Meanwhile, the high-
est accuracy of 94.71% is attained on 4-class task. PLV of high oscillatory IMFs outperforms the reported systems 
with conventional EEG features.

1  Introduction
Emotions play a vital role in human existence, shaping 
our interactions, perceptions, and overall psychological 
state. They have a profound impact on various aspects 
of our lives, including our relationships, daily experi-
ences, and overall well-being. Understanding and effec-
tively managing our emotions are crucial for maintaining 
optimal mental health and overall quality of life. Human 
emotion is a complex cognitive process related to the 
mood, thoughts, preferences, and behavior of an individ-
ual [1]. It can be evoked by external stimuli like listening 
to music, viewing photos, videos, or movies. Emotion is 
defined and represented either as discrete types or along 
multiple descriptive dimensions [2]. Psychologists stud-
ied different types of emotions, namely happiness, sad-
ness, surprise, fear, anger, and disgust [3]. Alternatively, 
emotional states can be categorized as positive, negative, 
or neutral [4]. A three-dimensional model was com-
monly adopted to describe emotion in terms of the levels 
of valence, arousal, and dominance [5]. Valence encom-
passes a pleasant to unpleasant state of emotion, while 
arousal refers to the intensity of emotion ranging from

boredom to excitement [5]. Dominance is the degree of

or disgust. A person’s affection or liking state is reflected 
in the positive or negative attitude expressed. In Russell’s 
circumplex model, emotional state is described in two 
bipolar dimensions: valence and arousal [6]. The present 
study is focused on the binary classification of valence, 
arousal, dominance, and liking, i.e., high state versus 
low state. Following the circumplex model of affect, we 
also tackle the four-class task: high valence high arousal 
(HVHA), high valence low arousal (HVLA), low valence 
high arousal (LVHA), and low valence low arousal 
(LVLA). These classes are associated with happiness, 
relaxation, anger, and sadness, respectively.
The emotional state of a person can be detected by ana-
lyzing physiological signals like electrocardiogram (ECG) 
[7] and EEG [8] or behavioral signals like voice [9] and/or 
face images [3]. The physical attributes of the ECG do not 
respond instantly to a change in emotion. For the modal-
ity of face image or natural speech, confusion caused by 
faked emotion could pose a major problem for practi-
cal use. EEG, captured via multiple electrodes placed on 
the scalp, measures voltage fluctuations among neuronal 
populations in the brain. Analyzing and detecting emo-
tional states with EEG signals can facilitate interactions 
between humans and intelligent devices, making it an 
important aspect of human-computer interaction (HCI). 
EEG signals are considered reliable and effective in 
detecting changes in emotional states because they pro-
vide instantaneous responses to emotion-evoked stimuli.
Traditional linear signal modeling techniques, such as 
auto-regressive models, Fourier transform, and wavelet 
transform, have been extensively utilized for processing 
and analyzing EEG signals [10–13]. Spectral analysis of 
EEG often involves the adoption of five prominent fre-
quency bands: delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha 
(8–14 Hz), beta (14–30 Hz), and gamma (above 30 Hz) 
[10, 14, 15]. Various spectral features, including signal 
power, spectral entropy, and others computed within 
these frequency bands, have been employed to investi-
gate different brain activities. However, due to the intri-
cate dynamics of the brain, EEG signals are believed to 
be generated through a time-varying and non-linear pro-
cess [16]. This implies that non-linear analysis techniques 
are required to extract meaningful features from EEG 
data. While the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) 
has been commonly used to obtain a temporal-spectral 
representation of non-stationary EEG signals [17, 18], it 
suffers from the limitation of using fixed window lengths. 
Short window lengths provide precise temporal infor-
mation but poor frequency resolution, while long win-
dow lengths offer good frequency resolution but poor 
temporal resolution. The wavelet transform provides 
low-frequency resolution at high frequencies and low-
time resolution at low frequencies. In both Fourier and 
wavelet analyses, pre-selected linear basis functions are 
employed [19]. In addition, STFT and continuous wave-
let transform (CWT) can only maintain either temporal 
or spectral resolution, making it challenging to obtain 
accurate time-frequency information simultaneously in 
EEG analysis [20].
In this study, we have applied a signal-dependent 
non-linear decomposition approach for EEG analysis. A 
univariate decomposition approach for multivariate sig-
nals like EEG can lead to a loss of joint channel proper-
ties after decomposition. To address this issue, we have 
tackled the multidimensional decomposition approach 
for multi-channel signals. Multi-channel EEG signals are 
analyzed using the Hilbert–Huang transform (HHT), 
which is a non-linear approach. The HHT algorithm per-
forms coherent time-frequency analysis and can achieve 
a proper balance of time and frequency resolution [21]. It 
starts with the process of empirical mode decomposition 
(EMD), by which a single-channel EEG signal is decom-
posed into a set of intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) based 
on the signal’s local characteristics. Applying single-
channel EMD straightforwardly to multi-channel signals 
leads to the issue of scale misalignment among the IMFs 
of different channels [22]. Mode-mixing might also occur 
within a particular channel [22, 23]. These problems can 
be alleviated by using the noise-assisted multivariate 
EMD (NA-MEMD) [23]. With NA-MEMD, each IMF 
carries spectral information in a specific frequency range. 
Applying the Hilbert transform to the IMF generates an 
analytic signal, which is specified in terms of instantane-
ous energy and phase. Hilbert spectral analysis gives the 
Hilbert spectrum, i.e., the time-frequency distribution 
of signal energy. It is a non-normalized weighted distri-
bution, while the weight at each time-frequency com-
ponent indicates the local energy. The marginal Hilbert 
spectrum (MHS) of each EEG channel provides valuable 
information about the energy contribution from differ-
ent frequency components. It represents the cumulative 
amplitude or energy across the entire segment of the sig-
nal, offering insights from a probabilistic perspective [24]. 
Unlike the Fourier spectrum, where energy at a frequency 
denotes its persistence throughout the signal, the pres-
ence of energy at a specific frequency in the MHS sug-
gests the likelihood of a local oscillation occurring at that 
frequency during the signal’s duration. Consequently, the 
MHS captures local spectral features rather than global 
ones, enhancing the effectiveness of EEG analysis.
Functional activities related to changes in emotion 
involve different brain regions. The importance of spatial 
information in multi-channel EEG was investigated in 
[25–27]. One focus of our research is on understanding

This method demonstrates the interdependence between

two primary measures used to show the mutual interde-
pendence between signals. Linear time-domain param-
eters named Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) were 
computed from multichannel EEG for functional con-
nectivity analysis to show connectivity between left-right 
hemispheres and different cortical regions, i.e., fron-
tal, central, parietal, and occipital regions [28]. The fre-
quency domain feature named partial directed coherence 
(PDC) was computed from different frequency bands of 
EEG using a linear approach [29]. Some studies observed 
that phase-information-based synchronization measures 
are more sensitive than amplitude-based measures, and 
these synchronization measures in different brain regions 
are non-linear [30]. To capture these asymmetric EEG 
parameters and obtain the connectivity network, phase 
synchronization analysis is performed on multichan-
nel EEG in this study. The phase synchronization index 
parameter (PSI), namely the phase locking value (PLV), 
is estimated from the instantaneous phase difference 
between two EEG channels. The estimated PLVs reveal 
the connectivity pattern in the brain at a specific time 
instant. The PLVs are used to build the functional con-
nectivity map, which describes the spatial relationship 
among each EEG channel. The effectiveness of these spa-
tial connectivity features is compared with MHS in the 
task of emotion classification.
A hybrid neural network consisting of 2D CNN and bi-
directional LSTM is utilized to model the MHS of all EEG 
channels to show the effectiveness of Hilbert spectral 
analysis. The use of the PLV in functional connectivity 
maps would be further investigated to demonstrate the 
efficacy of connectivity pattern analysis in detecting emo-
tion variation. In this work, noise-assisted multivariate 
empirical mode decomposition and the Hilbert Huang 
transform are performed using MATLAB software. The 
feature representations used for the emotion detection 
study are prepared with MATLAB 2019a. To perform 
detection and classification, the deep learning framework 
is used. The training and testing are performed using 
Python and its associated package modules. The main 
contributions of this study can be highlighted as follows:
•	 Developing a novel noise-assisted MEMD-HHT-
based emotion detection approach using MHS of 
multi-channel EEG;
•	 Proposing to use non-linear features to construct a 
connectivity map;
•	 Demonstrating the importance of phase information 
in functional connectivity analysis to indicate inher-
ent brain activity associated with emotion variation.

2  Related work
The key components of a signal classification system 
comprise feature extraction, feature selection, and a 
machine learning model. Numerous types of temporal, 
spectral, and temporal-spectral EEG features were pro-
posed and investigated. Power spectral density (PSD) and 
differential entropy (DE) were obtained by Fourier analy-
sis [10]. Auto-regressive models were applied to estimate 
the PSD of EEG [11]. CWT was applied to individual 
EEG channels to characterize functional brain activities 
with higher-order spectral features (HOS) [13, 31]. The 
discrete wavelet transform (DWT) decomposed a single-
channel EEG signal into several sub-bands, from which 
a textural feature pattern generation was proposed [32]. 
A game-based feature generation method named Tetro-
mino was utilized in their work, and it followed differ-
ent characters of the Tetris game to generate non-linear 
textural features. A tunable Q-factor wavelet transform 
(TQWT) was used to decompose an EEG signal into 
different sub-bands [33, 34]. A set of statistical features 
named moments was extracted from the decomposed 
signals. Moreover, an S-box of the Clefia cipher was uti-
lized to generate non-linear textural features. The cryp-
tographic S-Box can provide non-linearity to the system, 
while the nonlinear histogram-based feature generator, 
i.e., Clefia pattern, extracted the hidden nonlinear fea-
tures from EEG signals [34]. The statistical moments and 
textural features were fused to prepare the input feature 
vector. Moreover, other widely recognized non-linear 
methods, e.g., EMD and variational mode decomposi-
tion (VMD) produced statistical and spectral features 
from individual channels for emotion detection [35]. 
Non-linear features, e.g., higher-order crossing, fractal 
dimension, correlation dimension, Lyapunov exponent, 
and Hjorth parameter, were extracted from EEG signals 
in [36–38]. Authors in [39] show the potential of geomet-
ric features derived from the time-domain EEG signals 
for accurate detection between normal and depressed

In the case of emotion classification, machine learn-
ing methods including support vector machine (SVM),

attempted [10, 33, 34, 36–38]. Min-Redundancy-Max-

or analysis of variance (ANOVA) were applied to select

significant advantages over conventional classification

deal with high-dimensional data, making them appealing

spectrogram features. Long-short-term memory (LSTM)

utilized with pre-trained CNN, showing the effective-
ness of deep spectral features on emotion detection [52]. 
Some works also use geometric features to show the 
underlying EEG pattern. Authors in [53] integrate a CNN 
as a fundamental component in discerning EEG patterns 
associated with alcoholism. This neural network classifier 
is trained on dynamic and geometrical features extracted 
from EEG signals’ phase space, enabling the model to 
identify unique patterns indicative of alcohol-related 
brain activity. The output of the CNN shows the model’s 
efficiency in processing intricate EEG data and accu-
rately categorizing alcohol-related brain activity based 
on distinct features derived from EEG. DNN models use 
automated feature learning processes in the spatial, tem-
poral, and spectral domains, outperforming conventional 
classifiers such as Naive Bayes, SVM, and kNN. However, 
the main challenge in training deep neural network mod-
els is the requirement for a large amount of data, which 
is often difficult to obtain for EEG-based tasks. This data 
scarcity hinders the performance of deep neural network 
classifiers. To address this issue, transfer learning has 
gained attention in computer-aided medical diagnosis or 
classification tasks [29, 51, 54]. In many studies, transfer 
learning has proven to be a highly effective strategy for 
efficiently tackling the issue of limited training data [46, 
47]. Transfer learning involves using pre-trained models 
to perform classification in a new domain. It can acceler-
ate the training process and overcome the challenges of 
limited training data and the high costs associated with 
building training models from scratch. The large num-
ber of layers in convolutional neural networks allows 
for the learning of deep features for better classification. 
Conversely, the extensive layering of the pretrained net-
work significantly increases model complexity and com-
putational costs, posing challenges in adapting features 
to a new domain. A combined 2D CNN-BiLSTM model 
shows advantages over pre-trained models by allowing 
customization and adaptability to specific datasets, ena-
bling direct feature learning from the data, developing 
task-specific representations, avoiding transfer learning 
limitations and biases, and facilitating domain adapta-
tion through fine-tuning. Training the 2D CNN-BiLSTM 
model from the beginning enables it to acquire features 
specifically suited to the given task. It potentially leads to 
improved performance over pre-trained models that may 
not align well with the characteristics of our EEG data. 
To handle the issue of data scarcity, the generative adver-

model generated additional spectral features in the effec-
tive frequency bands of the EEG. The spectral features

3  Extraction of EEG features
3.1  IMF extraction with NA‑MEMD
The iterative sifting operation of EMD decomposes a uni-
variate signal into a set of IMFs [24]. Each IMF is an ampli-
tude-modulated and frequency-modulated signal. EMD 
is a data-driven operation without requiring pre-selected 
basis functions. To decompose a broad-band signal into 
IMFs, the local extremes of the signal are located, and the 
local mean is determined. To ensure a narrow-band IMF, 
the local mean of the signal envelope at any point will be 
zero. Moreover, the number of zero crossings and the 
extremes of the envelope will be equal or differ by one [24, 
57]. For a multivariate signal, EMD can be done indepen-
dently on individual dimensions. However, this would lead 
to the problem of non-uniformity across the IMFs, which 
in our application correspond to different EEG channels. 
The scale-misalignment problem occurs, i.e., frequency 
scales in IMFs with the same index may be inconsistent 
among the channels. Moreover, the single oscillatory mode 
resides in more than one IMF, causing mode mixing in the 
IMFs. The mode mixing problem hinders the achievement 
of the dyadic filter bank property of EMD [23]. The ensem-
ble EMD (EEMD) was proposed to address this problem 
by applying sifting to an ensemble of noise-added signals 
[58]. In this process, EMD is applied to every member of 
the resulting ensemble. The mean of IMFs with the same 
index across ensembles yields the decomposed IMFs, each 
of which carries a single oscillatory mode. The direct addi-
tion of noise to the original signal may cause noise interfer-
ence in the decomposed IMFs in the EEMD process [23]. 
On the other hand, the multivariate EMD (MEMD) makes 
use of spatial information via projection of the multivariate 
signal to extract common oscillatory modes across chan-
nels [54]. MEMD yields scale-aligned IMFs but inherits a 
certain degree of mode mixing.
To tackle the above problems all together, noise-assisted 
MEMD was proposed [22]. In NA-MEMD, m-channel 
independent white Gaussian noise signals are used in con-
junction with given n-channel EEG to produce an (n + m)
-variate signal. The noise signals are treated as individual 
channels rather than adding directly to the original signal 
[23]. The major steps of NA-MEMD are explained below 
[22].

4  Proposed design of emotion detection system
4.1  IMF selection
The application of NA-MEMD results in an equal num-
ber of IMFs across all EEG channels. However, it is 
important to note that not all IMFs are equally significant 
for emotion detection, as some can contain irrelevant 
and redundant information [61]. To address this issue, 
various criteria, such as correlation coefficient and aver-
age power, can be employed for IMF selection [61, 62]. 
To determine the relevance of each IMF to the raw EEG, 
the PCC is utilized, which measures the strength of the 
relationship between the two. IMFs that exhibit a strong 
correlation with the raw EEG are considered to carry 
essential information for this work. This study focuses 
on calculating the mean correlation coefficients between 
each IMF and the raw EEG across all channels. IMFs are 
primarily chosen based on their correlation coefficient, 
using a threshold of 0.3.
The research also explored the effectiveness of spectral 
features derived from high-frequency beta and gamma-
band EEG signals for emotion detection [27, 63]. How-
ever, it was observed that the low-frequency components 
played a more significant role in indicating sleep and 
resting states rather than emotion detection [64]. There-

were ultimately chosen to conduct the task of emotion 
detection.
4.2  Input feature preparation
The MHS and PLV are computed from narrow-band 
IMFs. For each channel, the IMF is divided into short 
segments. Each one-second-long EEG segment con-
tains 128 samples. The MHS is derived from each seg-
ment. The spectral energy contributed by the frequency 
components is obtained from MHS. By aggregating the 
spectral energy of EEG signals from all channels, a 2D 
representation is constructed. The 2D matrix has a size 
of C × W , where C is the number of EEG channels and 
W is the number of frequency components in MHS. By 
stacking the 2D frame of four consecutive segments, a 3D 
feature representation is obtained. The 3D block of size 
C × W × T yields spectral-temporal features of all EEG 
channels as input to the 2D CNN-BiLSTM model.

4.3  2D CNN‑BiLSTM model architecture
The feature extraction in the temporal and spatial 
domains can be performed simultaneously with a hybrid 
convolution-recurrent neural network model. The 
learned spatial-temporal features with the hybrid model 
show an advantage over spatial or temporal features mod-
eled by any 2D CNN or LSTM network. The architecture 
of 2D CNN-BiLSTM is depicted in Fig. 2. It comprises 
four convolution blocks and one bi-directional LSTM 
layer. Each block contains a layer with a 3 × 3 learnable 
convolution kernel. Each convolution layer is followed by 
a non-linear activation function, i.e., the Rectified Linear 
Unit (ReLU). The input channel depths of the convolu-
tion blocks are 4, 32, 64, and 128, while the output chan-
nels have depths of 32, 64, 128, and 128, respectively. At 
each layer, the 2D kernel performs convolution opera-
tions with the input features, and the result of convolu-
tion is passed through the activation ReLU to learn deep 
spatial features. 2D batch normalization is applied to 
accelerate model training and reduce the loss. A 2D max-
pooling with a 2 × 2 kernel is used after the fourth con-
volution layer. The output of CNN layers is the input of 
a BiLSTM with 128 hidden units to extract the tempo-
ral features. The input features in a BiLSTM cell flow in 
both forward and backward directions, preserving past 
and future information as well. After learning the tempo-
ral features, a flatten operation is performed to transform 
them into a one-dimensional (1D) vector. The 1D features 
are passed through a fully connected (FC) layer, followed 
by ReLU. A dropout rate of 0.25 is applied after each layer 
activation to avoid overfitting. Sigmoid and softmax acti-
vation functions are used after the second FC layer to 
make the final prediction of binary and multi-class tasks. 
Training was performed with a mini-batch size of 64. We 
have used the Adam optimizer with a 0.0001 initial learn-
ing rate and a cross-entropy loss function.
5  Experiments and results
5.1  Database and experimental setup
Different studies used multi-channel EEG datasets for 
EEG-based analysis and classification [65, 66]. In this 
study, experiments on emotion detection and classifica-
tion are carried out using a publicly available multi-chan-
nel EEG dataset named DEAP1 [67]. The dataset contains 
32-channel EEG signals acquired from 16 male and 16 
female healthy subjects. The ages of these subjects ranged 
from 19 to 37 years. Each of the subjects was arranged 
to view 40 video clips, resulting in the collection of 1280 
multichannel EEG signals for independent emotion anal-
ysis. For each video-watching session, a 1-min-long EEG 
was recorded and digitized using a sampling frequency 
of 500 Hz. After watching an emotion-evoking video, 
the subject was asked to provide a self-assessment score 
ranging from 1 to 9 to indicate “low” ( < 5 ) and “high” 
( > 5 ) states in valence, arousal, dominance, and liking 
levels. In our study, these self-assessment scores were 
used as ground-truth labels for machine learning model 
training and evaluation. Based on the ratings on valence 
and arousal, emotions are divided into four classes, i.e., 
HVHA, HVLA, LVHA, or LVLA, as described in the 
Introduction section.
The proposed methods are also validated on another 
dataset named SEED2 [27]. EEG signals in SEED com-
prise 62 channels. They were collected from 15 healthy 
subjects (7 male and 8 female, age: 23.27±2.37 year). 
Each participating subject was arranged to view 45 vid-
eos, from each of which a 4-min-long EEG was recorded. 
A total of 675 multichannel EEG signals were recorded. 
Emotion analysis was conducted on a per-video-trial 
basis, with participants watching the videos multiple 
times to elicit emotions. Based on the theme of the video 
stimulus, the evoked emotion is assigned to one of the 
three states: positive, negative, or neutral. These ground-
truth labels were used for model training.
Raw signals from DEAP and SEED were down-sampled 
to 128 Hz. Channel re-referencing was done by global 
averaging [68]. Fivefold cross-validation experiments 
were carried out across different subsets of data to ensure 
the generalization of the models. In each fold, 80% of the 
recording sessions were used for model training and 20% 
for testing. The 2D CNN-BiLSTM model was trained for 
300 iterations. The average accuracy of the fivefolds was 
calculated to give the overall model’s performance.

6  Discussion
Empirical wavelet transform is used in [82] for multi-
channel EEG signal analysis. In this study, the Noise-
Assisted Empirical Mode Decomposition (NA-MEMD) 
is preferred over linear techniques like Fast Fourier 
Transform (FFT) and wavelet due to its adaptability to 
non-stationary EEG signals and its capacity to offer a 
multi-scale representation of signal components. Unlike 
the use of predefined linear basis functions such as FFT 
and wavelet, NA-MEMD decomposes signals relying on 
their local information, capturing essential instantaneous 
local features crucial for EEG analysis. By leveraging 
noise assistance, NA-MEMD enhances mode separation, 
reduces mode mixing, and improves the clarity of the 
intrinsic mode functions derived from the input signals. 
Multivariate VMD is used in [83]. NA-MEMD and mul-
tivariate VMD are both used to decompose multivariate 
signals. NA-MEMD is suitable for signals with non-linear 
and adaptive characteristics where traditional decompo-
sition methods might not perform as effectively. Multi-
variate VMD, with its variational optimization approach, 
aims to find the decomposition that best represents the 
signal based on a specified criterion. It is effective for 
capturing signal features in a concise manner, but has 
limited capability for dealing with non-linearity.
The present study clearly shows the benefits of non-lin-
ear data-driven analysis methods for EEG signals. Aim-
ing to capture the local characteristics of multi-channel 
EEG, IMFs are extracted using NA-MEMD, which is 
more robust than conventional MEMD. It is noted that 
a small number of IMFs corresponding to high oscilla-
tory modes carry most of the required information for 
representing emotion changes. Specifically, MHS and 
PLV features extracted from the first five IMFs cover the 
frequency bands of 24–45 Hz, 13–24 Hz, 8–13 Hz, 4–8 
Hz and 2–4 Hz, respectively. Hilbert spectral analysis on 
the IMFs gives the Hilbert spectrum that has a complete 
time-frequency resolution. MHS is a one-dimensional

The mode-mixing problem of MEMD causes overlap-

The present study also demonstrates the use of func-
tional connectivity analysis to detect emotional states. 
Spatial connectivity analysis can capture the synchro-
nized communication between different regions of the 
brain, which is an important aspect of emotion process-
ing. This approach can identify patterns of interconnec-
tions among brain regions that are expected to be specific 
to different emotions. It provides insight into the neural 
mechanisms underlying emotional processing. Func-
tional connectivity analysis was applied to EEG [29] and 
functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) [84] in 
brain research. The brain EEG signal has a good temporal 
resolution as it can capture changes in brain activity over 
short time intervals. In our experiments, connectivity is 
given by a non-linear measure that indicates neuronal 
activation time and region in relation to changes in emo-
tion. The brain activation time and regions can provide 
a complete inner view while studying emotion due to 
its rapid induction and changes over time. The phase 
synchronization analysis has shown good sensitivity to 
emotional variation. The functional connectivity map 
constructed by PLV reflects internal functioning across 
brain regions. It shows an advantage over any other 
EEG-based non-linear features. PLV obtained from IMFs 
decomposed by NA-MEMD demonstrates notable bene-
fits over those provided by MEMD. This suggests that the 
mode-mixing problem can be alleviated by NA-MEMD. 
Each IMF corresponds to a specific sub-band of the EEG. 
It is expected that the phase-frequency relationship is dis-
tinct among different emotion states. It can be effectively 
obtained from the phase synchronization parameter. For 
a broad-band EEG signal (1–45 Hz), the phase synchro-
nization parameters are shown less discriminative in 
performing the intended classification task. The spatial 
connectivity parameters showed significance in reflecting 
the change in emotion for a particular frequency band 
signal at 24–45 Hz for IMF1. On the other hand, spec-
tral features from IMF1 in conjunction with IMF2 and 
IMF3 achieved notable performance on classification. 
Overall, our proposed non-linear signal modeling reveals 
significance in EEG analysis, while the marginal Hilbert 
spectrum and functional connectivity map are promising 
candidates for characterizing the brain wave for detecting 
emotion states.

tion of PCA to each subband independently to extract

7  Conclusion
This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the mar-
ginal Hilbert spectrum and functional connectivity 
map of multi-channel EEG in characterizing functional 
brain activity for emotion detection. The instantaneous 
spectral energy of high oscillating intrinsic mode func-
tions is found to be discriminative on the intended task. 
The efficacy of applying functional connectivity analysis 
is investigated with phase locking values. For the nar-
row-band signal, the phase synchronization parameters 
performed better than the spectral energy in detect-
ing emotion variation. These non-linear features can 
be successfully modeled by our hybrid neural network, 
showing the distinct benefit of the proposed approach 
over other LSTMs, pre-trained models, or 2D/3D 
CNN-based classifiers.
Next, we can explore the use of EEG-fMRI-based 
functional connectivity analysis to gain a more compre-
hensive understanding of the functional organization 
of the brain. EEG-based connectivity analysis examines 
the temporal correlation or phase synchrony between 
EEG signals recorded from different electrodes. How-
ever, EEG signals are influenced by activity throughout 
the entire brain, not just the regions directly beneath 
the electrodes. By combining EEG with fMRI, we can 
leverage the high temporal resolution of EEG and 
the high spatial resolution of fMRI. This integrated 
approach may offer the potential to obtain a more 
complete and accurate depiction of the connectivity 
between brain regions. It would allow us to identify 
specific brain regions that are specifically involved in 
particular cognitive or emotional processes. Further-
more, this approach can be promising for important 
clinical applications, particularly in the diagnosis and 
treatment of neurological and psychiatric disorders. It 
can provide an unprecedented opportunity to identify 
different subtypes of these disorders and track their 
progression over time.

Abstract: Emotion is an integral part of human cognitive processes and behaviors. Automatic detection and classification of human emotion has been a goal of applied research. This study presents an approach to detecting emotion from multivariate electroencephalogram (EEG) with signal processing methods applied in the temporal, spec- tral, and spatial domains. In this work, the noise-assisted multivariate empirical mode decomposition (NA-MEMD) is applied to EEG to extract a set of narrow-band intrinsic mode functions (IMF), upon which spectral analysis and spa- tial connectivity analysis are performed. Applying Hilbert spectral analysis to those IMFs results in the marginal Hilbert spectrum (MHS). MHS is computed for each EEG channel to obtain the spectral energy of each segment. The spec- tral energy across multiple EEG channels within the same segment is aggregated while the consecutive frames are stacked to give spectral-temporal feature representation. Again, connectivity analysis is performed at each instant with a non-linear measure named phase locking value (PLV) to construct the connectivity map containing spatial- temporal features. A 2D CNN-BiLSTM is adopted to perform emotion detection with the MHS and the PLV features. On classifying high versus low states in valence, arousal, dominance, and liking, PLV showed better performance than MHS with 97.61%, 96.09%, 96.75%, and 97.23% accuracy, respectively, for DEAP dataset. Meanwhile, the high- est accuracy of 94.71% is attained on 4-class task. PLV of high oscillatory IMFs outperforms the reported systems with conventional EEG features.
